demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't rely on other people
I can no longer trust my own body
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless the accident specifically involved a snake, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items point to generic post-traumatic cueing, but this item implies a highly specific trauma cue that lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another and is not supported by the other nodes. The profile otherwise centers on guilt, danger scanning, intrusive recollection, and distrust of self/body; betrayal by another person introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme without corroboration.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding emotional closeness/intimacy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The dominant threat and memory items concern danger, hypervigilance, intrusive imagery, numbness, and grief after an accidental injury event. Intimacy avoidance could occur, but here it appears to address an interpersonal/betrayal theme that is not otherwise coherently represented, especially given the unsupported betrayal appraisal.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by generalized interpersonal/environmental danger monitoring (avoiding unfamiliar places, scanning exits in any room), which fits assault or deliberate threat contexts better than accidentally causing serious injury to another in an accident. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly focused on accidents, loss of control, or harm recurrence rather than pervasive escape-oriented vigilance across all settings.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I can't rely on other people' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on accident-related triggers, guilt, bodily unreliability, and generalized hypervigilance, but there is no corresponding interpersonal betrayal, abandonment, or dependence theme to support this item. It stands out as clinically disconnected from the trauma narrative and the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
# Linh's Story

Linh was nineteen when the car hit her client. It was a Tuesday afternoon in late April, three years ago, at the corner salon where she'd been working as a hairdresser for just under a year. Mrs. Chen, a regular in her sixties, had stepped into the crosswalk after her appointment while Linh stood at the salon window, watching her leave. The delivery truck ran the red light. The sound—metal on bone, the wet crack of impact—came before Linh's mind could process what her eyes had seen. Mrs. Chen lay crumpled on the asphalt, her new perm still perfect, her leg bent at an angle that made Linh's stomach turn to ice. For three long seconds, Linh stood frozen, her hands still wet from the rinse bowl. She had shampooed that woman's hair. She had told her the color would bring out her eyes. She had let her walk out the door.

The first weeks after the accident were strange—Linh moved through them as if watching herself from outside her body. Mrs. Chen survived, though she spent two months in the hospital and would never walk without a cane. The guilt, though, felt like a physical weight that Linh carried into every room. She had come to believe, with absolute certainty, that she should have protected Mrs. Chen somehow—should have warned her, should have checked the street, should have done something other than stand there and watch. The conviction that she had failed, that she could have prevented it all, crystallized into a kind of moral certainty that made her shoulders ache. When she thought about that moment—and she thought about it constantly—she felt overwhelmed by a grief so thick it was hard to breathe. Other times, she could recall the exact sequence of events with perfect visual clarity, the truck's grille, Mrs. Chen's expression of surprise, but feel nothing at all, as if the memory belonged to someone else entirely.

The intrusive thoughts began within days. Unwanted images would surface without warning—the impact, the sound, Mrs. Chen's face—and Linh found herself unable to control their arrival or their intensity. When a car backfired outside the salon, or when a client dropped something heavy, the loud noise would send her heart racing, and suddenly she was back at the crosswalk, watching it happen again. The visual memories were so vivid and so frequent that Linh began to organize her life around avoiding the triggers that summoned them. She stopped driving entirely and refused rides from friends, convinced that being inside a vehicle made her complicit in some way, that she couldn't trust her own body to react correctly if danger came. She started taking the bus, which meant longer commutes, which meant arriving home exhausted and raw.

But the avoidance spread. She stopped going to the salon on the anniversary of the accident, calling in sick even though her manager had already covered the schedule twice before. She avoided loud environments altogether—no restaurants with open kitchens, no bars where friends wanted to celebrate birthdays. The list of places she couldn't enter grew longer each month. What frightened her most was the realization that she couldn't rely on other people to keep her safe, couldn't trust them to follow the rules of the road or to look both ways. This conviction fed back into her avoidance of driving, made it feel not like anxiety but like wisdom, like the only rational response to a world that had proven itself fundamentally unpredictable. She became hypervigilant in every space she entered, scanning for exits the moment she crossed a threshold, her body tense and ready to flee. Even in her apartment with her boyfriend Marco, she found herself unable to relax, always aware of where the door was, always half-listening for sirens.

The more she avoided, the more her negative appraisals hardened into unshakeable truths. Because she couldn't drive, because she couldn't go out on certain dates, because her body jolted at every loud noise, Linh became convinced that her own body had become unreliable—a betrayer that wouldn't obey her commands, wouldn't let her feel safe even when she was safe. Her belief that she had failed to protect Mrs. Chen began to generalize; she started becoming overly compliant with Marco and her family, apologizing for things that weren't her fault, agreeing to things she didn't want to do, as if perfect obedience might somehow prevent the next catastrophe. The guilt and the hypervigilance fed each other. Each time she scanned a room for exits, each time her heart raced at a siren, she felt the memory surface again—not just the visual image but the crushing sense that she had known, somehow, that something terrible would happen, and she had done nothing. The unwanted thoughts came more frequently, and with them came the physical reactivity: her hands shaking, her chest tight, her breath shallow. She was caught in a cycle she couldn't name but couldn't escape.

By the time Linh came to her first appointment, she hadn't driven in nearly three years. She'd turned down a promotion at the salon because it would require opening a second location across town. Her relationship with Marco had become strained; he didn't understand why she flinched at every honk, why she couldn't sit with her back to the window, why she had become so apologetic for things beyond her control. What brought her in, finally, was the realization that the anniversary of the accident was approaching again, and the thought of it made her want to disappear entirely. She was hoping someone could help her understand why her mind wouldn't let the memory go, why her body wouldn't believe her when she told it she was safe. But underneath that hope was a deeper fear: that she would never be able to trust herself again, that the person she had been before April—capable, present, able to let people walk out the door without catastrophe—was gone forever.
